catalog_quote: Normally, Bahinemo words contain a single stress accented syllable and are contained within the Pre-nuclear, Nuclear and Post Nuclear Phrases. There are two classes of words: accented words and nuclear words. [4.1 Nuclear words:] ... The peak of stress normally occurs on the first prefix on the grammatical verb and seldom occurs on the verb root itself. ... [4.2 Accented words:] Accented words have one accented syllable with the highest tone and heavier stress in the word. ... Few Bahinemo accented words have more than three syllables. ... Accented words are normally nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs and other words. All accented words have one syllable that is accented with the highest tone and stress in the word. All possible patterns occur in two and three syllable words, but there are only a few contrastive minimal pairs for stress accent observed. Final syllable stress is the predominant pattern on both two and three syllable words. All single syllable words are accented. Therefore, it is not necessary to write stress on these. [tables 4.3, printed pp. 5-6] Accent on: 1st syllable ... 2nd syllable ... 'man' ˈima ... 'girl' dəˈɸi ... 'many' ˈmajɸa ... 'bird' waˈbu ... Three syllable single words: Accented syllable: 1st ... 2nd ... 3rd ... 'to the man' ˈimama ... 'to the house' iˈnama ... 'ear' bəsiˈja

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every Bahinemo word has one accented syllable that carries both the heaviest stress and the word's highest tone (stress and tone coincide: 'tone-stress'). For nouns and other non-verb words the accent can fall on any syllable of a 2- or 3-syllable word and must be specified lexically (a few minimal pairs), with final-syllable accent the most frequent pattern; inflected verbs place the stress peak on the first prefix rather than the root, and bare verb roots lack a high tone. Monosyllables are always accented. Pitch realisation of the accent then depends on the word's position in the phonological phrase and sentence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described for the word; the source describes phrase-level prominence instead (head word of a noun phrase slightly stronger; one nuclear peak per phonological sentence, and a 'sentence stress' that the OPD calls phonemic and writes by underlining).
new_statements.exceptions: Position is not fixed: 'All possible patterns occur in two and three syllable words, but there are only a few contrastive minimal pairs for stress accent observed'; tables pp. 5-6 give 2-syllable words accented on 1st (ˈima 'man', ˈmaja 'many', ˈmija 'rib cage') vs 2nd (dˈi 'girl', waˈbu 'bird', miˈja 'tall') and 3-syllable words accented on 1st (ˈimama 'to the man', ˈbisia 'razor'), 2nd (iˈnama 'to the house', diˈnija 'sun') or 3rd (bsiˈja 'ear', baniˈja 'large'). Verbs: stress on first prefix, seldom on root; a verb root can become nuclear in two-root constructions. Bruce 1979:513-514 (citing Dye & Dye 1969) summarises the same as 'phonemic tone-stress.. may occur on any syllable in the word'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, embedded in a top-down phonological-sentence analysis: accented words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs) each carry one stress-accented syllable which is also the word's highest tone; nuclear words (inflected verbs) take the sentence-stress peak on the first verb prefix, not the root; uninflected verb roots have no high tone (OPD p. 3). Accent realisation (pitch level) is heavily conditioned by position in Pre-Nuclear / Nuclear / Post-Nuclear phrase (secs. 3, 4.3). In a noun phrase each word keeps its own accent but the head word is slightly stronger (4.2.1, p. 5). Single-syllable words are all accented. Orthography since 2007 writes no stress marks; the dictionary marks word stress with a high tone (8.1.1, pp. 27-28).
new_statements.identity_note: Both deciding files describe Bahinemo as spoken at Wagu village (Ambunti, East Sepik), the main Bahinemo village (Laycock 1973 no. 102 'BAHINEMO (Wogu)'); the OPD calls it 'Bahinemo (Gahom) Language [BJH]'. This is bahi1254 proper, not the distinct Wagu language wagu1234 (no ISO), although the PDFs were first saved under by that check and are now copied to the bahi1254 directory. Bruce 1979 spells it Bahinemo; older SIL MSS use 'Gahom/Ghaom'.

sources.note: p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': "Stress and tone work together on word level. Sentence stress is phonemic and must be. Tone is phonemic. There are two classes of words. Unaccented words which all are uninflected verb roots do not have a high tone. The prefix take stress. All other words have one high tone." Examples begá 'taro' / bega 'to play', gaidí 'round' / gaidi 'to wash', gelá 'flutes' / gela 'to sing'. p. 4: high tone written with acute; sentence stress underlined.

sources.note: Second-hand: "Dye and Dye (1969) give evidence for phonemic tone-stress in Bahinemo. Thus tone-stress must be specified for each word in Bahinemo and may occur on any syllable in the word." Also Bruce 1984 PL C-81 (held by the project) cites Dye & Dye 1965 'Gahom phonology' MS and 1969 'New interpretations of Bahinemo (Ghaom) phonology' MS, SIL Ukarumpa, for vowel allophony only.
